name: Pearl Blackberry
lede: Pearl Blackberry is a muted, greyish purple from the German RAL paint standard, and it lands close enough to our archive's Heather Grey that the two are a near-exact match.

sections.title: A pearl, qualified
sections.body:
Our library catalogues this name from RAL 4012, the industrial color-matching standard first issued in Germany in 1927, and flags it as an obscure, qualified name rather than a core teaching word [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[plumbago-slate]], [[deep-slate-violet]], [[campanula-purple]] and [[purplish-grey]], at 5.4, 5.5, 5.5 and 6.1 ΔE [1]. In Munsell terms it reads 9.8PB 4.4/3.2: low chroma, tipped toward blue-violet, and the ISCC-NBS system would call its block "grayish purple" [1].

The nearest named color in our data is [[heather-grey|Heather grey]], at a CIEDE2000 distance of 0.0 — the two names describe the same computed swatch [1]. No book in our library explains why RAL paired "pearl" with "blackberry" for this particular grey-violet; the pairing is undocumented here [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Pearl Blackberry appears in 77 of our 23,781 paintings, about 0.32 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it covering real area in 40 of them [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 2.9 times the expected rate for that century, and is most over-represented in French paintings, at 2.3 times expected [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, tucked in rather than carrying the light [2].

The earliest match in our archive is dated 1460, in a panel by Filippo Lippi — 467 years before RAL's 1927 record of the name, as photographed, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. That gap is a look-alike hue surviving in an aged photograph, not proof that anyone mixed this specific grey-violet that early [2].
